name: data_run_python
description:
Run sandboxed pandas (`pd`) / numpy (`np`) / scipy.stats over one or more tables, then
(optionally) write the result BACK to an enabled destination — a table, a spreadsheet, or a
downloadable file — all in one call. Row data lives where it is and is streamed to the sandbox;
only your `output` (a small summary you choose) crosses the wire.

## When to use this tool

This is the PRIMARY tool for reading, computing over, and writing tabular data — whether the
data lives in ONE source or spans several. Reach for it whenever the answer needs a
COMPUTATION (max/mean/filter/groupby/join/dedupe/diff/statistical test) or a WRITE-BACK
(append rows to a table, fill a formula down a spreadsheet, edit rows, export a file).
Cross-store tasks are one prominent case — "update the database from this spreadsheet",
"download this table as a CSV", "sync a spreadsheet with the DB", "compare this file against
the table" — but a single-source analytical question ("which product has the highest price in
this attachment?") is equally in scope. Do NOT read-and-eyeball a table to compare or aggregate
it — bind it and compute.

## Binding sources (`bindings`, required — at least one)

Each entry names a Python variable (`var`) and points at EXACTLY ONE source. All bindings are
fetched IN PARALLEL and bound as Python globals — each a list of `{col: val}` dicts — BEFORE
your `code` runs. Rebuild the DataFrame with `df = pd.DataFrame(var)`.

The enabled source fields depend on this deployment (see "Available sources" below):
  - `attachment_id` — a CSV/XLSX from the conversation catalog. XLSX only: optional
    `sheet_name` (default first tab) and `header_row` (1-indexed, default 1 — set 2 for a
    title row above the header).
  - `data` — an inline array of `{col: val}` objects (or a 2-D array with a header row).
    Use it to pass a table you produced yourself (e.g. one extracted from an image).

```python
# bindings: [
#   {"var": "sales",   "attachment_id": "doc_abc"},
#   {"var": "targets", "data": [{"sku": "A", "goal": 100}]}
# ]
sales   = pd.DataFrame(sales)
targets = pd.DataFrame(targets)
```

## `code` / `code_ref` and surfacing output

Supply the Python source ONE of two ways — exactly one is required:
  - `code` — Python source inline.

Either way, the code that runs is Python source. Pre-imported: `pd` (pandas), `np` (numpy),
`stats` (scipy.stats), and the stdlib (math, datetime, decimal, json, re, statistics, string,
collections, functools, itertools). Assign a global `output` (any JSON-serializable value) —
THAT is what you see back. DataFrames auto-convert via `to_dict(orient="records")`, Series via
`to_list()`, numpy scalars via `.item()`. Keep `output` SMALL — a count, a summary, a handful
of rows. Large result sets belong in a write sink (below), not in `output`.

## Write sinks — push results back out

Beyond `output`, assign any of the write-sink global dicts below, keyed by destination name.
Each value is EITHER a bare pandas DataFrame (uses that sink's default mode) OR a spec dict. In
a spec dict the DataFrame ALWAYS goes in a field literally named `df` — never any other name.
### `output_attachments` → downloadable file

Key = a filename ending in `.csv` or `.xlsx` (no other extension). Bare DataFrame, or
`{"df": df, "delimiter": ";"}` (CSV delimiter override). Returns `{name, document_id, rows,
bytes}` per file. Use it to hand the user a file they can download.

```python
output_attachments = {"reporte.csv": result_df,
                      "detalle.xlsx": {"df": detail_df}}
```

## Anti-patterns — read this before you compute

⚠️ KNOW THE COLUMNS FIRST. Binding a source loads its ROWS, not its schema. The catalog
auto-summary already shows each attachment/sheet's inferred columns + sample rows in your
system message — USE IT. If you don't already know the real column names and what each holds,
inspect first. Never guess a column name or what a term means (e.g. "frutas" is almost
certainly a VALUE in a `Categoria` column, not part of a product name). Guessing silently
produces wrong results — a filter matching 0 rows, or the wrong rows, with no error.

⚠️ SANITY-CHECK THE ROW COUNT. If a filter/groupby/mask matches 0 rows (or far fewer than you
expected), do NOT report success — that is a signal you misunderstood the data. Find the right
column/value and redo it.

⚠️ COERCE TYPES. All CSV and spreadsheet cell values arrive as STRINGS (pandas object dtype).
Before numeric ops, coerce: `df["price"] = pd.to_numeric(df["price"], errors="coerce")` or
`df = df.astype({"price": float, "stock": int})`. Comparing/sorting/summing string columns
silently gives lexical (not numeric) results. SQL-sourced bindings arrive already typed.

## Sandbox restrictions
  - Blocked imports: os, sys, subprocess, socket, urllib, requests, importlib, builtins, ctypes.
  - No filesystem access, no network access beyond the fetched bindings.
  - Code wall-clock capped; response truncated at a fixed byte limit; writes capped at 100k rows.

Available sources:
- Attachment (CSV/XLSX from the conversation catalog)
- Inline JSON data
summary: The pandas workbench for tabular data — read from files, spreadsheets, SQL, or inline JSON, compute, and write results back to any enabled destination. Rows never enter your context.

bindings.description: Tabular bindings to load. Each becomes a Python global (a list of `{col: val}` dicts) under the name given by `var`. At least one entry required. Bindings are fetched IN PARALLEL, each from its own source (attachment, Google Sheets, SQL `SELECT`, or inline JSON data).

items.description: One tabular binding: a Python variable name plus exactly one data source. The active source is determined structurally by [`classify_binding`] — no explicit `source` discriminator field is required from the LLM.

var.description: Python variable name to bind the records to (e.g. "products"). Accepts UX aliases `binding_name` and `name`.

sheet.description: Google Sheets tab name (gsheets source). NOT aliased to `sheet_name` — that field is reserved for the attachment-XLSX tab selector below; the two sources are structurally distinct.

range.description: Optional A1 range (gsheets source only). Omit to read the entire tab.

data.description: Inline table data — an array of `{col: val}` objects, or a 2-D array whose first row is the header (inline source).

delimiter.description: CSV delimiter override (attachment source, CSV only).

sheet_name.description: XLSX tab/sheet selector (attachment source, XLSX only). Distinct from `sheet` (gsheets tab) — do not conflate the two.

code.description: Python code, inline. Has access to `pandas as pd`, `numpy as np`, `scipy.stats as stats`, plus each binding's records list bound under its `var` name. Define `output` (any JSON-serializable value) — that is what the LLM sees. Exactly one of `code` or `code_ref` must be set.

code_ref.description: Reference key for stored code, resolved server-side via the operator-only `fixed_config.code_source_query` SQL binding instead of pasting code inline. Exactly one of `code` or `code_ref` must be set. Requires the operator to have configured `code_source_query` (and a `sql` capability) on this tool instance.

write_to_spreadsheet.description: Optional target spreadsheet for `output_sheets` returned by the script (Google Sheets sink). Only meaningful when the `gsheets` capability is enabled.

on_existing_sheet.description: Operator-set collision policy for `output_sheets` (`fail` | `auto_suffix` | `overwrite`). Sourced from `fixed_config.on_existing_sheet` — the executor wrapper injects it into the args before [`dispatch_core`] runs. Mirrors `gsheets_run_python`'s field of the same name.
